name: Eye Trace Continuity Cut
additional_sources: knowledge/research/transcripts/what not to do in editing.txt
use_when: The edit should feel smooth and easy to follow.
A cut moves between shots with important visual information.
The viewer might otherwise need to search the frame after the cut.
A montage, city-entering sequence, or walk-and-talk uses many shots and needs smooth orientation.
The edit feels rushed because the focal point changes before the viewer can scan it.
The subject action should stay center-frame so the viewer can follow it without re-searching.
A talking-head punch-in or crop is used to hide a jump cut without making the eyes teleport.
A short-form opener uses centered face guides or a match cut so an angle change feels smooth.
avoid_when: The desired effect is shock, confusion, or visual rupture.
A composition intentionally hides information for suspense.
The next shot's key information must be discovered slowly.
A jarring cut or visual rupture is emotionally intentional.

timeline_pattern.position_rule: Track where the viewer's eye is likely to be at the cut and place or guide the next key information accordingly.
timeline_pattern.review_rule: Review the cut at phone size and normal speed to ensure the eye does not have to hunt.
timeline_pattern.movement_rule: For smooth B-roll strings, keep camera or subject movement direction consistent unless a direction change has story purpose.
timeline_pattern.focal_point_rule: Each shot should have an obvious focal point before the cut occurs.
timeline_pattern.action_center_rule: For small objects, hand actions, or demonstrations, keep the action center-frame unless off-center framing has a purpose.
timeline_pattern.face_center_rule: When a face carries the hook or emotional continuity, align the face to center or a stable guide across cuts.

motion.rule: Use pan, zoom, scale, crop, or object motion to guide attention from the old eye position to the new one.

keyframe_values.subtle_reframe_duration: 6-12 frames for fast social edits, 12-24 frames for calmer edits
keyframe_values.scale_change: Typically 3-8% when used only to guide attention
keyframe_values.talking_head_punch_in: Use a subtle 105-115% scale change when hiding a jump cut; align eyes and mouth as closely as possible.
keyframe_values.centered_face_match: For early short-form angle changes, keep the face near the same center/eyeline guide before and after the cut.
keyframe_values.easing: Ease out into the key information rather than snapping unless a jolt is intended
keyframe_values.direction_match: Prefer same-direction movement across adjacent shots; horizontal flips are acceptable only when they do not misrepresent text, geography, or truth.

sound.rule: Keep audio smooth so the visual continuity is not undermined by an accidental audio jump.

captions.rule: Place captions so they do not pull the eye away from the next key visual point.
captions.use: Caption position can guide the eye when the caption is the key information.

color.rule: Use contrast and brightness to make the next key information easy to find.
color.avoid: Grade jumps that force the viewer to re-orient.

implementation.ffmpeg: Use crop, scale, overlay guides, or contact sheets to compare final eye position before the cut and first key information after the cut. Render small A/B tests for timing. Use hflip only when reversing direction does not falsify readable signs, maps, or geography.
implementation.remotion: Store key visual regions as x/y metadata and animate crop or overlay placement to maintain continuity.
implementation.blender: Use camera framing and motion paths to move attention predictably between compositions.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Use crop/position keyframes or choose a different shot where the subject appears near the previous focal area.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use safe guides, comparison view, and motion keyframes to align focal points across cuts.

common_mistakes: Ignoring where the viewer was looking before the cut.
Cutting before the viewer has time to scan the focal point.
Mixing left-to-right and right-to-left motion randomly in a sequence meant to feel smooth.
Putting captions over the visual path the viewer needs to follow.
Using flashy transitions when simple spatial continuity would be smoother.
Reviewing only on a large monitor and missing phone-size search time.
Using a punch-in that makes the speaker's eyes jump to a new screen position without motivation.
Ignoring face-center guides during the first hook cuts of a short.
qc: Can the viewer find the next key information immediately?
Does the cut feel smooth at normal speed?
Do captions or graphics compete with the intended focal point?
Does color or contrast help the eye land in the right place?
Does every shot have a clear focal point before the cut?
Does small-object action stay centered or deliberately guided?
Are movement directions consistent or intentionally contrasted?
If a punch-in hides a cut, do the eyes and mouth remain close enough that the cut feels natural?
During early hook cuts, does the face stay aligned enough that the angle change feels smooth?
